solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: A battle royal, commonly speaking? (8,5)

blocks.note: the surface reading: a free-for-all fight, fists and all
the setter's reading: a battle fought in common speech, in insults and rough language

annotation.surface: A dictionary-style gloss on the phrase battle royal, as ordinary people would put it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Commonly speaking' looks like a note on register, but it hints at slang: this battle is fought with words rather than fists.
annotation.definitionFit: A battle royal is a fierce dispute, and a slanging match is a noisy exchange of insults.

entries.clue: High ball to catch however, drop the ball dog! (4,7)

indicatorNotes.to catch: the skier catches the next two pieces, holding them inside it

blocks.note: in cricket a skier is a catch hit very high
to drop the ball is to make a mistake, to err

annotation.surface: A fielder's frustration at a spilled high catch, before shouting at a dog on the pitch.
annotation.walkthrough: A skier is a cricket term for a ball hit high in the air. All the cricket talk is there to hide a Scottish breed of terrier.
annotation.definitionFit: The Skye terrier is a long-haired Scottish breed of dog.

entries.clue: Last of silage fed to a sheep, swallowed (3,2)

indicatorNotes.Last of: take the final letter of silage
indicatorNotes.fed to: the E goes inside the sheep, as food would

blocks.note: final letter of silage, placed after the first letter of the sheep

annotation.surface: A farmer watching the dregs of the silage vanish into a sheep.
annotation.walkthrough: A tup is a ram, a farm word few solvers outside Britain know; silage is fermented grass fed to livestock.
annotation.definitionFit: To eat up something is to swallow the lot.

entries.clue: Military campaign where one supports launching of ball into Bastille? (9)

indicatorNotes.launching of: in a down clue, launching sends the word upwards, so it reads backwards
indicatorNotes.into: the reversed ball goes into the prison
indicatorNotes.supports: in a down clue, the I sits underneath and so holds up the rest

blocks.note: the Bastille was a Paris prison; gaol is the British spelling of jail
a pill is a small ball

annotation.surface: Someone backing a ball being lobbed over the walls of the Bastille, as if the storming were a game.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Launching' reverses only because this is a down clue: the ball goes up the grid. 'Supports' likewise places a letter underneath only in a down clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Gallipoli was the Allied First World War campaign on the Dardanelles peninsula in 1915.

entries.clue: Songs: they’ll knock you out (7)

blocks.note: a song in a show is a number
things that make you numb, such as sedatives or anaesthetics

annotation.surface: A reviewer saying the songs in a show are knockouts.
annotation.walkthrough: The second definition means sedatives, things that numb; the surface wants it to mean the songs are stunning.
annotation.definitionFit: A musical number is a song, and a numb-er would be something that knocks you out.

entries.clue: 20 across, champ! (5)

blocks.note: 20 across is ARTIST, so a painter is wanted: the Norwegian who painted The Scream
to champ is to chew noisily

annotation.walkthrough: 'Champ' looks like a champion, but it is the verb, to chew noisily.
annotation.definitionFit: Munch is an artist, and to munch or champ is to chew noisily.

entries.clue: Modern hit composed in Nordic city (9)

indicatorNotes.composed: the letters are put together, as a composer arranges notes

annotation.surface: A pop song written in a Scandinavian city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Composed' fits the song surface so well that it is easy to miss as the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Trondheim, Norway's third-largest city, is one Nordic city.

entries.clue: Hurry off for audition? (3)

indicatorNotes.for audition: an audition is a hearing, so we want what is heard

blocks.note: meat or game that has gone off is high

annotation.surface: An actor rushing off to try out for a part.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Off' reads as leaving, but it means gone bad, as high game is.
annotation.definitionFit: An archaic synonym: hie survives mainly in poetry and in 'hie thee hence'.

entries.clue: Breed kennelled by royalty, Pekinese (4)

indicatorNotes.kennelled by: the answer is housed inside the following words, as a dog is in a kennel

annotation.surface: A breed of dog kept by the royal family, the Pekinese.
annotation.walkthrough: The Pekinese really was a Chinese imperial dog, so the surface reads as fact while the answer straddles two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a breed of dog is one kind of dog.

entries.clue: Swimmer, one chasing loser (5,4)

indicatorNotes.chasing: SOLE comes after LEMON, as a chaser comes behind

blocks.note: a lemon is a dud or failure

annotation.surface: A race where one swimmer trails behind the last-placed competitor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' is a fish, not a racer.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this flatfish is one of many creatures crosswords call a swimmer.

entries.clue: A source of water and basic food for a packet (2,1,5)

annotation.surface: Survival supplies of water and staple food in a packet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Packet' looks like packaging, but 'costing a packet' is British slang for costing a lot of money.
annotation.definitionFit: Something bought for a packet was bought at a price, at great cost.

entries.clue: Barking hounds bay (6)

indicatorNotes.Barking: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters are scrambled

annotation.surface: Hounds baying, which is exactly the noise hounds make.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bay' looks like the verb for a hound's cry; it is the noun, Hudson Bay in Canada.
annotation.definitionFit: Hudson Bay is a large bay in northern Canada.

entries.clue: Old player swollen and sore having been fouled (5,6)

indicatorNotes.having been fouled: fouled means messed up, so the letters are disordered

blocks.note: anagram fodder is SWOLLEN and SORE, 11 letters; 'and' just joins them

annotation.surface: A veteran footballer left bruised and swollen after a foul.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Player' and 'fouled' paint a sportsman, but a player is also an actor.
annotation.definitionFit: Orson Welles was an actor of the last century, so an old player.

entries.clue: Well, I’m polite? (8,2)

blocks.note: read literally: gracious, that is polite, describes me

annotation.surface: A slightly hesitant claim to good manners.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second half is the answer read literally rather than a true definition.
annotation.definitionFit: "Gracious me!" is an exclamation like "Well!", and gracious means polite.

entries.clue: Kittens? Something for them to go on! (3,6)

annotation.definition2: Something for them to go on!

blocks.note: a cat's litter is its brood of kittens

blocks.clueFragment: Something for them to go on!
blocks.note: the grit in a cat's toilet tray

annotation.surface: Kittens and the tray they are trained to use.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go' is the euphemism for relieving oneself, and 'them' ties the second sense back to the kittens of the first.
annotation.definitionFit: A cat's litter is its kittens, and cat litter is the grit in a cat's toilet tray.

entries.clue: Duty: useless excuse to have one put on a cross (6,3)

annotation.surface: A grumble that some obligation is a feeble excuse for crucifying someone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Useless' splits as use-less: remove those three letters from the excuse.
annotation.definitionFit: An excise tax is a duty charged on goods such as alcohol.

entries.clue: Where capital unavailable, rent facility (4)

indicatorNotes.capital unavailable: the capital, or first letter, is not there

blocks.note: to lease is to rent; drop the L

annotation.surface: A lending scheme for when money is short.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like money for a loan; it is the capital letter at the start.
annotation.definitionFit: Facility means ease, as in doing something with facility.

entries.clue: Perfect, time and time again (4)

blocks.note: min = minute, a period of time

annotation.surface: Praise for something done perfectly every time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Time and time again' looks like an idiom for repeatedly; it asks for two separate times.
annotation.definitionFit: From coins fresh from the Mint: 'in mint condition' means unused and flawless.

entries.clue: Bribe church staff to stop popular service finishing early (10)

indicatorNotes.to stop: CE MEN plugs the gap in DUT, stopping it up
indicatorNotes.finishing early: DUTY ends one letter too soon, losing the Y

annotation.surface: Paying off the clergy to cancel a popular service.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like a priest's crook; here it is the workforce. 'Popular service' reads as one phrase but splits in two.
annotation.definitionFit: An inducement is a bribe, something offered to persuade.

entries.clue: Avant-garde movement angry about hosting platform (7)

indicatorNotes.about: about means turned around, so MAD is read in reverse
indicatorNotes.hosting: DAM holds DAIS inside, as a host has a guest

blocks.note: a dais is a raised platform

annotation.surface: An art movement furious over the platform it has been given.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Angry about' reads as one phrase in the surface, but 'about' is the signal to turn angry round.
annotation.definitionFit: Dadaism was the anti-art movement of the early twentieth century.

entries.clue: Trinkets primarily observed inside, grandee having failed to close drawer, say? (6)

indicatorNotes.primarily: primarily means first of all, so take the first letter
indicatorNotes.observed inside: the T is seen within the grandee, placed inside it
indicatorNotes.having failed to close: a word that fails to close never reaches its end, so ARISTO loses its last letter

blocks.note: ARISTO, short for aristocrat, without its last letter

annotation.surface: A noble who cannot shut a drawer full of trinkets, so they are seen inside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drawer' is not furniture but someone who draws, and the question mark flags the pun. Aristo is informal British for an aristocrat.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who draws is an example of an artist.

entries.clue: National University in Nordic city (5)

blocks.note: a Turk is a national of Turkey

annotation.surface: A national university located in a Scandinavian city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'National University' reads as one name; it splits into a person and an abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Turku, Finland's former capital, is one Nordic city.

entries.clue: Diplomatic individual caught on tape (8)

indicatorNotes.caught on tape: a tape recording captures sound, so we want what is heard

annotation.surface: A tactful diplomat who is secretly recorded.
annotation.walkthrough: The two spellings are pronounced the same but mean different things, so only the sound carries over.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a careful, tactful person keeps things quiet, which is what diplomacy asks.

entries.clue: Stack bordering large field (5)

indicatorNotes.bordering: REAM lies on both sides of the L

blocks.note: a ream is a stack of paper
L = large, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: A haystack at the edge of a big field.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Field' is not farmland but an area of interest.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: a field of study is a domain, as in 'the realm of physics'.

entries.clue: Service provider broadcast its URL: it contains glitches initially (9)

indicatorNotes.contains: the rearranged letters hold the G inside
indicatorNotes.initially: initially means at the start, so take the opening letter

annotation.surface: An internet provider posting its web address, which has bugs from the start.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Service provider' sounds like broadband, but the service is a church one. The colon is surface punctuation; 'it' belongs in the anagram fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A liturgist writes or leads liturgy, the form of a church service.

entries.clue: Remove coating of dark resin (3)

indicatorNotes.Remove coating of: strip the outside letters, leaving the core

blocks.note: black = dark; drop B and K

annotation.surface: Instructions for stripping off a dark varnish.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface fits the answer, since lac is used to make varnish.
annotation.definitionFit: Lac is a resin secreted by an insect, the source of shellac.

entries.clue: Feller perhaps keeping third of bullets in revolver? (4)

indicatorNotes.keeping: to keep something is to hold it, so AXE holds the L inside
indicatorNotes.third of: third of means the letter standing in third place

annotation.surface: A gunman loading bullets into a revolver.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Feller' reads as a fellow and 'revolver' as a gun; really a felling tool and something that revolves.
annotation.definitionFit: An axle turns, so it is a revolver of sorts, hence the question mark.

entries.clue: Rowdy group saw you and me in Roman arena (6,7)

blocks.note: a circus is a noisy, chaotic crowd
a saw is an old saying

annotation.surface: Someone recalling watching a rowdy crowd with a friend at the Colosseum.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see; it is the noun for a proverb.
annotation.definitionFit: The Circus Maximus was the great chariot-racing arena of ancient Rome.
